Family Health

Missed a contraceptive pill? Timing, backup and next steps

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A missed pill is common and does not automatically mean pregnancy. The next step depends on the exact pill, how late it is, how many active tablets were missed, the position in the pack and when sex occurred. Find your pack and leaflet now. If pregnancy-risk sex has already happened, ask a pharmacist or contraception service promptly about emergency contraception rather than waiting for bleeding or a pregnancy test. If you have already taken ulipristal emergency contraception, obtain its restart instructions before taking more hormonal pills.

Start with the product and the clock

Check the name and active ingredients, whether each missed tablet contained hormones, the scheduled dose times, the last tablets actually taken and any recent pill-free interval. Tell the adviser about sex without reliable protection, vomiting, severe diarrhoea and other medicines or herbal products. Colour alone cannot identify a tablet across brands. If the timing or pill type is uncertain, use condoms correctly or avoid pregnancy-risk sex while getting specific advice.

Combined pills contain estrogen and a progestogen; progestogen-only pills include traditional, desogestrel and drospirenone products. Their rules differ. The examples below identify the guidance being described, because professional recommendations and local product leaflets are not always identical. Follow a plan matched to your actual product and circumstances; do not combine the shortest time window from one source with the shortest backup interval from another.

One late or missed standard combined pill

In the CDC’s standard combined-pill guidance, a tablet is late when less than 24 hours have passed since it was due. One missed active tablet is 24 to less than 48 hours late. Take it as soon as possible and continue the remaining tablets at the usual time, even if this means two on the same day. Additional contraception is generally not needed for this isolated error. This example is not an instruction to override a product-specific leaflet or an emergency-contraception restart plan.

Earlier errors can change the assessment. Emergency contraception is not usually needed for one isolated missed tablet, but the CDC advises considering it in selected situations involving other misses earlier in the cycle or the previous pack’s final active week. Special formulations, including multiphasic pills and some 24/4 products, need their own instructions. For example, Qlaira has day-specific rules and sometimes nine days of backup; do not apply a generic seven-day rule to every combined pill.

Two or more combined pills, and errors near the break

In the CDC example, two or more consecutive active pills missed means at least 48 hours since a pill should have been taken. Take the most recent missed tablet promptly, discard earlier missed tablets and continue the pack at the normal time. Use condoms or avoid pregnancy-risk sex until active tablets have been taken for seven consecutive days. Do not take two tablets every day for several days to catch up, or apply a blanket fourteen-day backup rule.

If these misses occur in the final active week, the standard CDC plan is to finish the active tablets and start the next pack the following day, omitting the hormone-free break or placebos. If a new pack cannot start immediately, backup is needed until seven consecutive active tablets from the new pack have been taken. Errors just after a break are particularly important: if pills were missed in the first week and pregnancy-risk sex occurred in the previous five days, seek emergency-contraception advice promptly. Longer interruptions or earlier errors require an individual plan, not simply waiting for the next period.

Inactive tablets and different pack schedules

Missing a genuinely hormone-free placebo does not itself remove hormone protection. Discard the forgotten inactive tablet and keep the next active pack on schedule; do not add extra inactive days while trying to finish every tablet. Check the leaflet to distinguish active and inactive tablets, especially in packs with several colours. Some everyday packs have two, four or seven placebos; other regimens have no planned break.

A late start to the next active pack is different from a forgotten placebo and may need missed-active-pill advice, backup and emergency contraception. Traditional and desogestrel progestogen-only packs usually contain active tablets taken continuously, while common drospirenone packs contain 24 active and four inactive tablets. Never assume that every mini-pill has no placebos or that the fourth week is always inactive.

Traditional progestogen-only pills

For traditional pills such as norethindrone/norethisterone, norgestrel or levonorgestrel products, the usual permitted delay is three hours. If a tablet is taken within the product’s window, take it when remembered and continue normally. Under CDC guidance for norethindrone or norgestrel, more than three hours late counts as missed: take one tablet promptly, then continue at the usual time, even if two are taken on the same day.

Use condoms or avoid pregnancy-risk sex until tablets have been taken correctly and on time for two consecutive days. FSRH professional guidance also uses 48 hours of backup after restarting traditional pills correctly. Sex during the lapse or before protection returns may require emergency contraception. The timing of sex, correct use before the error and whether this was a first start matter; do not assume that all sex in the previous week has the same risk or that no advice is needed.

Desogestrel: a twelve-hour window, with differing backup advice

Desogestrel pills have a twelve-hour window rather than the traditional three-hour window. If more than twelve hours late, FSRH professional guidance advises taking the most recent missed tablet, continuing normally and using condoms or avoiding pregnancy-risk sex for 48 hours after correct use restarts. Earlier missed tablets do not all need to be swallowed. Ask promptly whether sex during the lapse requires emergency contraception.

The Cerazette patient leaflet gives seven days of additional contraception after a delay of more than twelve hours. This is a real difference from the professional 48-hour recommendation, not a reason to choose a shorter interval yourself. Follow your product’s instructions while a pharmacist or clinician confirms the plan appropriate to you. Missing a full day does not create one universal seven-day rule for every mini-pill.

Drospirenone: check which instructions apply

Drospirenone-only pills commonly have 24 active tablets followed by four placebos and a wider timing window. UK FSRH guidance treats an active tablet at least 24 hours late as missed, and advises taking the most recent missed tablet, continuing daily and using condoms or avoiding pregnancy-risk sex for seven consecutive active-pill days. If a miss involves the final seven active tablets, its plan omits the placebos and starts the next active pack without that interval. Recent sex and misses around the break need individual assessment.

US CDC guidance differs: one late or missed active drospirenone tablet less than 48 hours after its scheduled time generally needs no additional protection after taking it and continuing. Two or more consecutive active tablets missed, at least 48 hours after a scheduled dose, require seven consecutive active-pill days of backup. The UK Slynd product information is more cautious after a delay exceeding 24 hours. Use your local product-specific plan; these are not interchangeable algorithms, and placebo errors must not extend the active-pill gap.

Recent sex and emergency contraception

Ask for same-day advice if protection may have lapsed and sex has occurred; do not wait to see whether a period comes. A copper IUD is the most effective emergency option and can provide ongoing contraception. It is commonly inserted within five days of the first pregnancy-risk sex, with other timing options in selected circumstances assessed by a clinician. Oral emergency contraception should be considered as soon as possible; available products and their licensed time limits differ.

Ulipristal is used within 120 hours. UK guidance describes levonorgestrel’s licensed 72-hour window and selected use beyond that, whereas CDC professional guidance discusses emergency pills within five days. This does not make every pill equally effective at every time. Recent progestogen use, interacting medicines, weight and the need to restart regular pills affect selection. Do not improvise a high-dose regimen from ordinary contraceptive tablets or take different emergency products together. Tell the adviser the exact pill and doses already taken.

Restarting after an emergency pill

Levonorgestrel emergency contraception usually allows immediate continuation or restart of the regular pill. Ulipristal usually requires waiting at least five full days, or 120 hours, before restarting a hormonal pill because progestogens can reduce its effect. Use condoms correctly or avoid pregnancy-risk sex throughout that waiting period and afterwards until the regular method is effective. An emergency pill does not protect sex later in the cycle.

Get the restart date and backup end date written down for your formulation. FSRH guidance generally uses two days after restarting traditional or desogestrel pills, seven for drospirenone or most combined pills, and nine for Qlaira; CDC emergency-contraception guidance generally uses seven days after restart. There is also a narrowly defined UK specialist exception allowing immediate combined-pill restart after ulipristal in a particular first-week missed-pill situation. Do not apply that exception yourself: seek a clear individual plan, including what to do if you already restarted or had sex again.

Pregnancy risk and when to test

A missed tablet does not guarantee ovulation or pregnancy, and no annual effectiveness percentage calculates the risk of one error. NHS estimates describe both combined and progestogen-only pills as over 99% effective with perfect use and about 91% with typical use over the first year. CDC estimates about seven pregnancies per 100 combined-hormonal users in a year of typical use. Different population estimates are not a personal forecast or a reason to blame yourself.

Arrange a pregnancy test 21 days after the last pregnancy-risk sex when advised after a lapse, even if bleeding has occurred. Test earlier if a period is missed as instructed, but an early negative cannot exclude a more recent pregnancy; further sex may require a later repeat. Pill hormones do not stop a pregnancy test working. Do not delay emergency-contraception advice until a test can become positive, and seek review after a positive result or persistent concern despite repeat negatives.

Bleeding, nausea and returning period symptoms

Missing tablets can cause spotting or withdrawal bleeding, earlier or irregular bleeding, heavier bleeding than usual on the pill, or a light or absent expected bleed. Symptoms that the pill previously controlled, such as painful or heavy periods or premenstrual symptoms, may return. Responses vary; a specific number of disturbed cycles is not guaranteed. Taking an extra tablet as directed can cause nausea, vomiting or bleeding.

Bleeding does not prove that contraception worked or exclude pregnancy. Seek clinical advice for persistent, new or troublesome bleeding, bleeding after sex, or bleeding that is heavy or prolonged. A clinician may check pregnancy, infection, the pill routine or other causes. Do not add extra pill-free days, repeatedly double doses or stop and restart packs to force bleeding; those changes can create further gaps in protection.

Backup methods, vomiting and interacting medicines

For missed-pill backup, use condoms correctly every time or avoid pregnancy-risk sex for the required interval. NHS annual estimates for external condoms are 98% with perfect use and 82% with typical use; internal condoms are 95% and 79%. These are year-long figures, not the protection from one act. Withdrawal, calendar counting or spermicide alone should not replace the condom or abstinence plan given for a pill error. Pills and emergency contraception do not protect against sexually transmitted infections; condoms reduce that risk.

Vomiting soon after a dose, severe or prolonged diarrhoea and some interacting medicines can reduce protection even without a forgotten tablet. Replacement-tablet timing and backup rules depend on the product and illness; check its leaflet and ask a pharmacist. Tell them about medicines for epilepsy, tuberculosis or HIV, and herbal products such as St John’s wort, without stopping essential treatment yourself. Advice for a simple isolated miss may not cover illness or a drug interaction.

Make the next dose easier to remember

Link the dose to a reliable daily routine, set a reminder and record when you actually take it so that you do not accidentally repeat a dose. A discreet visual cue can help. Keep sufficient supplies and, if suitable, a spare intact pack available for time away from home; check expiry dates. Follow the blister order and storage instructions. Do not automatically move tablets into a loose organiser or a humid bathroom: some packaging protects against moisture and light and preserves the active-placebo sequence.

Before travel across time zones, plan with a pharmacist how to keep the correct interval for your pill; the same local clock time is not always the same interval. Check whether a phone alarm changes time zone automatically. Carry tablets in their protective packaging and avoid storage conditions outside the leaflet. If daily dosing often does not fit your life, ask about another method, including an implant or IUD, without pressure to choose one. Keep condoms and your missed-pill instructions accessible.

Warning signs need care, not another pill

Get urgent medical advice for possible pregnancy with pelvic or abdominal pain, or an unusual bleed with a missed period; an ectopic pregnancy is possible even before a positive test. Shoulder-tip pain with possible pregnancy needs advice right away and does not require simultaneous pelvic pain. If pregnancy is established, contact maternity care immediately about any vaginal bleeding. Do not assume these symptoms are just withdrawal bleeding.

Severe or worsening pelvic pain, or pain that hurts with movement or touch, needs immediate emergency assessment. Pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or heavy vaginal bleeding also needs emergency care. Heavy bleeding with chest pain, breathlessness or marked dizziness is another emergency warning. If pregnant, heavy bleeding alone also requires emergency help. Do not drive yourself. Seek help without waiting for a reminder, an app entry, the next pill or a pregnancy-test date.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Have your exact pack, active ingredients, scheduled and actual dose times, pack day, illness or other medicines, and dates of sex ready when you ask for advice. Use condoms or avoid pregnancy-risk sex if the applicable plan is uncertain.

Ask promptly about emergency contraception after a possible lapse. Get written restart and backup end dates, especially after ulipristal; protect the entire waiting period and the time until your regular method is effective.

Arrange the advised pregnancy test and assessment of persistent or unusual bleeding. Use reminders and suitable storage to support your chosen method, but seek urgent care for warning signs without waiting for the next tablet.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record pill times, bleeding, reminders and questions for a pharmacist or clinician. It cannot identify a tablet from its colour, calculate the pregnancy risk of a missed dose or choose emergency contraception and restart instructions. Urgent advice and treatment take priority over recording data.

When to seek help

Do not use a generic catch-up schedule for every pill or repeatedly double doses. Seek prompt advice after pregnancy-risk sex, and clarify restart timing if ulipristal was used. Possible pregnancy with pain or unusual bleeding needs urgent assessment; shoulder-tip pain needs advice right away. Severe or worsening pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with fainting or loss of consciousness, breathing difficulty or heavy bleeding, requires immediate emergency care. Heavy bleeding in an established pregnancy also requires emergency care. Do not drive yourself or wait for a pregnancy-test date.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Identify the exact pill, active tablets, scheduled times, pack position and dates of sex before choosing a missed-dose plan.
  • Combined, traditional, desogestrel and drospirenone pills have different rules; product leaflets and professional guidance can differ.
  • Do not repeatedly double doses or extend a hormone-free interval; use the backup interval matched to your plan.
  • Seek emergency-contraception advice promptly and get explicit restart instructions, including protection throughout any ulipristal wait.
  • Bleeding is not proof of protection; arrange testing after pregnancy-risk sex and seek urgent help for warning signs.

Frequently asked questions

Can a missed pill cause side effects?

It can cause spotting, irregular or withdrawal bleeding, a heavier or lighter expected bleed, or return of symptoms previously controlled by the pill. An extra tablet taken as directed may cause nausea or bleeding. Effects vary. Persistent, heavy or unusual bleeding needs assessment; severe or worsening pelvic pain, fainting or loss of consciousness, breathing difficulty, or heavy bleeding with marked dizziness requires immediate emergency care.

Is there a fixed time limit to make up a combined pill?

There is no universal deadline after which nothing can be done. CDC standard guidance distinguishes one active pill less than 48 hours after it was due from two or more consecutive misses at least 48 hours after a scheduled dose. Product-specific rules can differ. Take the appropriate next step promptly with your leaflet or pharmacist, including backup and emergency-contraception assessment when needed; do not simply wait for a new period.

Will I become pregnant if I forget a pill?

Not necessarily. The risk depends on the pill, length and position of the interruption, previous correct use and timing of sex. Misses near a hormone-free break can matter particularly. No bleeding pattern or annual effectiveness number gives your exact risk. Ask promptly about emergency contraception if protection may have lapsed, and arrange a test 21 days after the last pregnancy-risk sex.

What can irregular combined-pill use do to my periods?

Spotting, earlier or irregular bleeding, heavier bleeding than usual on treatment, a lighter or absent bleed and returning premenstrual or period symptoms can occur. They are not inevitable and do not confirm or exclude pregnancy. Seek advice for troublesome or persistent changes rather than repeatedly changing doses or adding breaks; heavy bleeding or pain with possible pregnancy needs timely assessment.

Do all mini-pills have the same three-hour rule?

No. Traditional products usually have a three-hour window, desogestrel twelve hours and drospirenone a wider window. The action after a miss also differs: FSRH professional backup is usually 48 hours for traditional/desogestrel and seven active-pill days for drospirenone, while some product leaflets and US recommendations differ. Identify your product and confirm the applicable plan instead of applying one mini-pill rule to all.

What if I forgot an inactive tablet?

A genuinely hormone-free placebo can be discarded without itself reducing protection, provided the next active tablets start on time. Do not extend the placebo interval to finish forgotten tablets. A delayed active pack is a different error. Use the leaflet, not colour alone, to identify inactive tablets.

Can I restart immediately after an emergency pill?

Usually after levonorgestrel, but generally not after ulipristal: it normally requires at least 120 hours before hormonal restart. Use condoms or avoid pregnancy-risk sex throughout the wait and until your specific pill becomes effective after restart. Backup duration and rare specialist exceptions vary, so ask for written dates. Do not assume an emergency pill protects sex afterwards.

How can I avoid another missed dose?

Use a dependable routine, a reminder and a record of actual doses; keep supplies and the leaflet available. Preserve blister order and product-specific storage rather than putting every pill loose in an organiser. Plan time-zone changes with a pharmacist to maintain the right interval. If daily pills are hard to manage, discuss alternatives without blame or pressure.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
